newsitem.title: USA: Centocor drug said effective at 6 months.
newsitem.headline: Centocor drug said effective at 6 months.

text.p: A study showed that Centocor Inc's blood-clot fighting drug ReoPro maintained its effectiveness in reducing deaths and heart attacks in angioplasty patients six months after the procedure, researchers said on Sunday.

Researchers from The Cleveland Clinic and Duke University Medical Center said ReoPro combined with low-dose heparin reduced the number of deaths and heart attacks by 46 percent six months after angioplasty. The results came when ReoPro was compared with a standard dose of heparin, a common drug used against blood clots, with a placebo.
The need for urgent revascularization procedures was cut by about 54 percent, they said.
The ReoPro data was unveiled at a crowded presentation at the American Heart Association's annual scientific sessions here.

The six-month data from the so-called EPILOG trial, followed earlier data from the study that showed that within 30 days after angioplasty, ReoPro reduced heart attacks and death by nearly 70 percent.

ReoPro, which is sold by Centocor's partner Eli Lilly and Co, was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in late 1994 but only for use in patients undergoing angioplasty with a high risk for abrupt artery closure. Angioplasty involves opening a clogged blood vessel with a tiny balloon.

Biotechnology analysts have said they expect Malvern, Penn.-based Centocor to file with the FDA by the end of the year to expand ReoPro's use to all angioplasty patients based on the favorable trial data.

"The benefit and safety of ReoPro for some angioplasty patients irrespective of risk is clear, but the cost effectiveness of this treatment for use in all patients must still be analyzed," said Eric Topol, chairman of the Cleveland Clinic's Department of Cardiology and chairman of the EPILOG study, said in a statement.
Analysts have said the $1,350 cost per treatment of ReoPro has been a barrier to its use.
Centocor said it plans to release cost-effectiveness data from the EPILOG trial in early 1997.
